newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Early euphoria fizzles out on mixed Asia markets.
newsitem.headline: Early euphoria fizzles out on mixed Asia markets.

text.p: Asian markets on Thursday took a wild ride on post-U.S. election euphoria, but a record high in Hong Kong and a 400-point surge in Tokyo had all but evaporated by midday and both bourses ended the day in negative territory.
Other Asian markets continued a rally that began after Tuesday's re-election of a Democratic president and a Republican congress.
The U.S. election news and a stable outlook for U.S. economic policy and interest rates drove the Dow Industrials up 96.53 points overnight to a record close of 6,177.71.

The Dow's overnight success prompted an early surge after the opening in Hong Kong. But stocks zigzagged throughout the day to close lower as fears of profit-taking on Wall Street set in, brokers said.
"After the rallies yesterday, the Dow Jones and the Hang Seng are looking toppish," said a broker with a Swiss institution in Hong Kong.
The Hang Seng Index closed down 40.21 points or 0.31 percent at 12,735.26 after setting a new intra-day high of 12,898.30 in early morning trading.

Tokyo stocks also gave up early gains. The Nikkei closed sharply lower after buying momentum carried over from the previous day was watered down by the yen's rises against the dollar and sporadic sales by foreign investors, brokers said.
They said Ryutaro Hashimoto's re-election as prime minister by Japan's Lower House of parliament, announced shortly before the market closed, provided little buying incentive.
The key 225-share Nikkei average slipped 220.41 points or 1.05 percent to finish at 20,771.11.
Manila managed to hang on to its gains as blue chips and selected second-liners were snapped up amid heavy volume. The main index closed up 64.63 points or 2.16 percent at 3,063.06.
"We have very aggressive buying. People were just eager to participate on account of the Dow Jones rise," said Felix Barrientos, trader at ING Barings Securities.
Other Asian market rallied mainly on domestic news.

Jakarta shares rose across the board by midsession in active foreign-led buying of selected big-capitalised counters, brokers said. The composite index ended the morning session up 8.55 points or 1.46 percent at 595.89 points.
Kuala Lumpur shares extended their gains but were off the morning highs. The Composite Index was up 2.96 points to 1,182.05 at midday, after hitting a morning high of 1,186.56.

The Singapore share market was propelled higher by foreign fund purchases of selected blue-chips, while Thai stocks climbed as foreign buyers and retail investors focused on the finance and banking sectors.
In New Zealand, the NZSE-40 Capital Index ended 13.68 points or 0.59 percent higher at 2,338.89 after profit-takers moved in to topple the index from its 2,353.09 peak.
Australian shares ignored the Dow's gain and focused instead on the gloomy earnings outlook for Australian companies. The All Ordinaries index closed down 13.9 points or 0.59 percent at 2,346.7.
Seoul shares ended down after profit-taking set in during the afternoon session, paring away earlier gains. The composite stock index ended down 5.53 points or 0.74 percent at a provisional 741.76.

Taiwan share prices closed lower as profit-taking swept the market in late trade, snapping a weeklong winning streak, brokers said. The weighted index closed 23.97 points or 0.36 percent lower at 6,629.68.
Brokers said bullishness in some markets from Wall Street's record high did not impress Taiwan investors.
"I don't think too many investors really considered Wall Street's rise and the U.S. election as big factors," said Wang Jieh, analyst for Foremost Investment.
The dollar plunged in Tokyo as comments from an influential Finance Ministry official led participants to believe Japan had altered its policy of seeking a strong dollar, dealers said.
The greenback started Asian trade at 113.80 yen, but found itself tumbling to as low as 112.01 yen by late Tokyo trade.
At 0846 GMT, the dollar traded at 112.28/2.33 yen and 1.5070/80 marks.
